channel.title: SARS-CoV-2: A History Run-Through
channel.description: A chronological walk through the SARS-CoV-2 literature, 2020 to the present — one landmark paper per episode, in the order it was published, with a focus on genomics.
channel.itunes:author: Nigel

item.title: Episode 9: The Architecture of SARS-CoV-2 Transcriptome — Cell, 23 April 2020
item.description:
Kim et al., "The Architecture of SARS-CoV-2 Transcriptome." Cell, 23 April 2020. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2020.04.011
The first experimental map of what the SARS-CoV-2 genome actually transcribes inside a cell. At the end of April 2020, Dongwan Kim, Hyeshik Chang and V. Narry Kim at Seoul National University and the Institute for Basic Science in Korea paired two orthogonal sequencing platforms — Oxford Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS, long single-molecule native-RNA reads with 3' bias) and MGI DNBseq (short-read, 300M-read deep coverage) — on total RNA from Vero cells infected with the Korean isolate BetaCoV/Korea/KCDC03/2020. The dual platform confirmed the nine canonical subgenomic RNAs (S, 3a, E, M, 6, 7a, 7b, 8, N) plus full-length genomic RNA, with nucleocapsid the most abundant transcript, and showed that ORF10 is essentially never expressed (1 of ~millions of DNBseq junction-spanning reads, 0 DRS reads) — the annotation should be reconsidered. They mapped a large population of noncanonical fusion transcripts in three classes (TRS-L-dependent noncanonical, TRS-L-independent long-distance, and TRS-L-independent local), accounting in aggregate for a substantial fraction of viral reads and producing predicted truncated or alternative protein products. Using poreplex, they measured per-molecule poly(A) tail lengths (median 47 nt, bimodal ~30/~45 nt subpeaks). Critically, they ran unmodified in-vitro-transcribed RNAs through the same nanopore pipeline as a control for base-modification detection — showing that Tombo's control-free 5mC calls were almost entirely false positives — then used sample-vs-sample comparison to identify 41 real modification sites enriched at an AAGAA-like motif and concentrated in positions 28,500–29,500. Longer sgRNAs carried more modifications than shorter ones, and heavily modified molecules carried systematically shorter poly(A) tails (Mann-Whitney p < 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻¹²), linking internal RNA modification to 3' turnover. m6A (no RRACH motif), ADAR editing (no A-to-G in DNBseq), and m1A (no RT stop) were excluded as the chemistry; the identity of the modification was left open. This episode walks through the DRS vs DNBseq complementarity, the discontinuous-transcription / TRS mechanism, the ORF10 verdict, the three classes of noncanonical junctions, the IVT-control trick for modification calling, and the modification–poly(A) coupling — all from the standpoint of what was known at the end of April 2020.

item.title: Episode 8: A SARS-CoV-2 protein interaction map reveals targets for drug repurposing — Nature, 30 April 2020
item.description:
Gordon et al., "A SARS-CoV-2 protein interaction map reveals targets for drug repurposing." Nature, 30 April 2020. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2286-9
The first systematic host-directed drug-repurposing effort against SARS-CoV-2. At the end of April 2020, with the pandemic now global and the only approved therapy (remdesivir) delivering only a modest effect, David Gordon, Nevan Krogan and a 100-plus-author consortium centred at UCSF's Quantitative Biosciences Institute, with the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and the Institut Pasteur, published the first proteome-scale SARS-CoV-2–human protein interaction map. They cloned, 2xStrep-tagged and expressed 26 of the 29 SARS-CoV-2 proteins in HEK293T cells and used affinity-purification mass spectrometry to pull down their human partners, identifying 332 high-confidence virus–host interactions. The interactome was enriched for vesicle trafficking, nuclear transport (including the Orf6 hijack of the NUP98/RAE1 mRNA export pathway), innate immune signalling, ribosome and translation machinery, ubiquitin ligases, and bromodomain-containing chromatin regulators. They then overlaid the host hits onto the chemical landscape, matching 66 druggable human proteins to 69 compounds (29 FDA-approved, 12 in clinical trials, 28 preclinical) and tested 47 of them against authentic SARS-CoV-2 in Vero E6 at Mount Sinai (immunofluorescence) and Institut Pasteur (qRT-PCR). Two chemical classes consistently blocked replication: translation inhibitors targeting the eIF4A cap-binding complex (zotatifin, ternatin-4) and sigma-1/sigma-2 receptor ligands (PB28, PD-144418, clemastine, hydroxychloroquine). The sigma arm included a sharp mechanistic argument: sigma-1 agonists reduced viral titre while the sigma-1 antagonist dextromethorphan increased it, and the paper flagged that hydroxychloroquine's ~30-fold sigma/hERG selectivity (vs. 500–5000× for dedicated sigma tools like PB28) made it a dangerous instrument for engaging sigma receptors clinically. This episode walks through the AP-MS pipeline and the SAINTexpress/MiST scoring, the biological themes in the 332-interaction map, the chemoinformatics-to-BSL3 pipeline that got 47 compounds into live-virus assays in weeks, and the specific hits in the translation and sigma arms — all from the standpoint of what was known at the end of April 2020.

item.title: Episode 7: SARS-CoV-2 Cell Entry Depends on ACE2 and TMPRSS2 and Is Blocked by a Clinically Proven Protease Inhibitor — Cell, 5 March 2020
item.description:
Hoffmann et al., "SARS-CoV-2 Cell Entry Depends on ACE2 and TMPRSS2 and Is Blocked by a Clinically Proven Protease Inhibitor." Cell, 5 March 2020. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2020.02.052
The entry pathway, and the first repurposed drug. In early March 2020, six days before the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, Markus Hoffmann, Stefan Pöhlmann and Christian Drosten and colleagues published the paper that defined how the new coronavirus gets into a cell — and in the same breath nominated an already-approved drug to block it. Using VSV pseudotypes carrying the SARS-CoV-2 spike, they showed that the new virus uses the same receptor as SARS-CoV: angiotensin-converting enzyme 2, ACE2. They then showed that spike priming, the proteolytic cut that releases the fusion machinery, can go through either of two routes — endosomal cathepsin B and L, or the plasma-membrane serine protease TMPRSS2 — and that in human lung cells and primary airway epithelial cells, TMPRSS2 is the operative route. Camostat mesylate, a clinically approved TMPRSS2 inhibitor used in Japan for pancreatitis, blocked spike-driven entry into those cells and reduced infection of Calu-3 cells by authentic SARS-CoV-2. They also showed that convalescent sera from SARS patients cross-neutralise the new virus, albeit at lower efficiency, and they flagged the new multibasic furin cleavage site at the S1/S2 junction as a notable difference from SARS-CoV. This episode walks through the VSV pseudotype assay, the BHK-21 receptor-swap experiments, the ammonium-chloride/E-64d/camostat protease dissection, and what it meant in March 2020 to point at a drug that was already on the shelf — all from the standpoint of what was known at the time of publication.

item.title: Episode 6: Structural basis of receptor recognition by SARS-CoV-2 — Nature, 30 March 2020
item.description:
Shang et al., "Structural basis of receptor recognition by SARS-CoV-2." Nature, 30 March 2020. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2179-y
The companion crystal structure to Episode 5. In late March 2020, as New York became the global epicenter and most of Europe went into lockdown, Jian Shang, Fang Li and colleagues at the University of Minnesota published a 2.68-angstrom X-ray crystal structure of the SARS-CoV-2 receptor binding domain bound to the human ACE2 peptidase domain. To get crystals, they grafted the SARS-CoV-2 receptor binding motif onto the SARS-CoV RBD scaffold — the business end was all new virus, but the surrounding fold crystallised the way they knew it could. The Li group had been studying how SARS-CoV engages ACE2 since 2005; they brought with them the vocabulary of two "hotspots" on ACE2 — hotspot-31 (the Lys31–Glu35 buried salt bridge) and hotspot-353 (the Lys353–Asp38 buried salt bridge) — whose stabilisation by the virus largely dictates whether a sarbecovirus can use the human receptor. The structure shows that two SARS-CoV-2 residues, Gln493 and Asn501, engage those two hotspots better than SARS-CoV did, and that a reconfigured four-residue ridge (Gly-Val-Glu-Gly in place of Pro-Pro-Ala) plus a Leu-to-Phe change at position 486 together tighten contact with the ACE2 alpha-1 helix. They also tested RaTG13, the closest bat relative of SARS-CoV-2: it already binds human ACE2 weakly, and three substitutions at the hotspot-interacting positions bring it close to the pandemic virus's affinity. This episode walks through the hotspot framework, the scaffold-grafting trick, the atomic contact map, the SPR and pull-down experiments, and the RaTG13 result that bears on the zoonotic origin question — all from the standpoint of what was known at the time of publication.

item.title: Episode 5: Structural basis for the recognition of SARS-CoV-2 by full-length human ACE2 — Science, 4 March 2020
item.description:
Yan et al., "Structural basis for the recognition of SARS-CoV-2 by full-length human ACE2." Science, 4 March 2020. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abb2762
The first atomic-level view of the receptor. In early March 2020, days before the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, Renhong Yan, Qiang Zhou and colleagues at Westlake University solved two cryo-electron microscopy structures: full-length human ACE2 at 2.9 angstroms, and the SARS-CoV-2 receptor binding domain bound to that same full-length ACE2, also at 2.9 angstroms. To stabilise ACE2 — a single-transmembrane protein that is otherwise too floppy for high-resolution reconstruction — they co-expressed it with its known chaperone partner, the amino-acid transporter B0AT1, which contributes bulk and anchors the complex in the membrane. The structure revealed that full-length ACE2 is an obligate dimer locked together by a previously unseen neck domain, that the dimer can hinge between open and closed states, and that one ACE2 dimer can simultaneously accommodate two spike trimers — but only when each engaging RBD is in the up conformation Wrapp and McLellan had reported two weeks earlier. A residue-by-residue comparison with the equivalent SARS-CoV complex pinpoints specific changes — notably Lys417 gaining a salt bridge with ACE2 Asp30, and Phe486 enlarging a hydrophobic contact — that help explain the ten-to-twenty-fold tighter binding reported for the new virus's spike. This episode walks through the B0AT1 scaffolding trick, the cryo-EM pipeline, the open/closed dimer dynamics, the atomic-level map of the virus–receptor interface, and what the structure said in March 2020 about receptor engagement — all from the standpoint of what was known at the time of publication.

item.title: Episode 4: The proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2 — Nature Medicine, 17 March 2020
item.description:
Andersen et al., "The proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2." Nature Medicine, 17 March 2020. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-020-0820-9
The first origin-of-the-virus paper in a top journal. In mid-March 2020, less than a week after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, Kristian Andersen, Andrew Rambaut, Ian Lipkin, Eddie Holmes and Robert Garry published a Perspective in Nature Medicine arguing from genomic data that SARS-CoV-2 was neither a purposefully engineered virus nor plausibly the product of cell-culture or animal passage in a lab. Their case rests on two features of the spike: a receptor binding domain whose high-affinity grip on human ACE2 uses a different residue solution than pre-pandemic computational models had predicted an engineered RBD would use, and a brand-new polybasic furin cleavage site at the S1/S2 junction with three predicted O-linked glycans around it, absent from every sampled bat or pangolin sarbecovirus. They lay out two natural scenarios — adaptation in an animal host before zoonotic transfer, or adaptation in humans after an initial cruder jump during a period of undetected transmission — and decline to pick between them given the data available at the time. This episode walks through the genomic comparison, the furin cleavage site and glycan argument, the recombination fingerprint from the pangolin receptor binding domain, and the specific logic the authors use to push the laboratory scenarios off the table — all from the standpoint of what was known in March 2020.

item.title: Episode 3: Cryo-EM structure of the 2019-nCoV spike in the prefusion conformation — Science, 19 February 2020
item.description:
Wrapp et al., "Cryo-EM structure of the 2019-nCoV spike in the prefusion conformation." Science, 19 February 2020. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abb2507
The show leaves genomics for structural biology. In February 2020, Daniel Wrapp, Jason McLellan and colleagues at the University of Texas at Austin solved the first atomic-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structure of the SARS-CoV-2 spike ectodomain in its prefusion conformation, at 3.5 angstroms. The construct carried the two-proline stabilising mutations McLellan's group had previously worked out for RSV and other coronaviruses — the design that went on to become the antigen in essentially every spike-targeting COVID vaccine. The map showed the trimer predominantly in a one-up-two-down receptor-binding-domain arrangement, surface plasmon resonance put the spike-ACE2 equilibrium dissociation constant at about 15 nanomolar — roughly 10- to 20-fold tighter than SARS-CoV spike binds the same receptor — and three published SARS-CoV antibodies failed to bind the new receptor-binding domain. This episode walks through why the prefusion state is the vaccine target, how the 2P stabilisation works, how cryo-EM at this resolution is done, and what the up-versus-down RBD dynamic means for both receptor engagement and antibody recognition — all from the standpoint of what was known at the time of publication.

item.title: Episode 2: A pneumonia outbreak associated with a new coronavirus of probable bat origin — Nature, 3 February 2020
item.description:
Zhou et al., "A pneumonia outbreak associated with a new coronavirus of probable bat origin." Nature, 3 February 2020. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2012-7
The companion report to Episode 1. In February 2020, Peng Zhou, Xing-Lou Yang, Xian-Guang Wang, Zheng-Li Shi and colleagues at the Wuhan Institute of Virology recovered five full-length genomes of the new coronavirus from seven ICU patients in Wuhan, independently confirming the Wu et al. report. They then pulled a previously-sampled bat coronavirus, RaTG13, from a horseshoe bat in Yunnan out of their archive, sequenced it in full, and showed it was 96.2% identical to the new virus across the whole genome — the closest known relative. The paper is best remembered for the receptor-usage experiment that showed the new virus uses human ACE2 to enter cells, which set the target for essentially every COVID vaccine and monoclonal antibody that followed. This episode walks through the pan-coronavirus PCR screen, the metagenomic genome assembly, the RaTG13 phylogenetic placement, the spike receptor-binding motif comparison, and the HeLa-cell ACE2 transfection assay — all from the standpoint of what was known at the time of publication.

item.title: Episode 1: A new coronavirus associated with human respiratory disease in China — Nature, 3 February 2020
item.description:
Wu et al., "A new coronavirus associated with human respiratory disease in China." Nature, 3 February 2020. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2008-3
The first episode of SARS-CoV-2: A History Run-Through. In February 2020, Fan Wu, Yong-Zhen Zhang, Edward Holmes, and colleagues published one of the first two Nature reports characterizing the novel coronavirus behind the Wuhan pneumonia cluster. Using unbiased meta-transcriptomic sequencing on a single bronchoalveolar lavage sample, they recovered the complete 29,903-nucleotide genome of a previously unknown sarbecovirus — most closely related to a bat SARS-like coronavirus at the whole-genome level, and bearing a receptor binding domain that looked built to grip human ACE2. This episode walks through why meta-transcriptomic sequencing was the right methodological choice, how the phylogenetic placement and recombination analysis were done, and what the receptor binding domain comparison allowed the authors to predict about human transmission — all from the standpoint of what was known at the time of publication.
